channel.title: Text_to_speech on Best of AI
channel.description: Recent content in Text_to_speech on Best of AI

item.title: Azure AI Speech
item.description:
Azure AI Speech brings Microsoft’s speech technology into applications. Speech-to-text transcribes audio in real time or from recordings in many languages, with options for custom vocabulary and speaker separation. Text-to-speech offers a large library of neural voices in many languages and styles, with control over tone, speed, and emotion using SSML. Real-time speech translation converts spoken language into another language for captions or voice.

Additional features serve specialized needs. Custom Neural Voice lets approved customers build a branded voice from recorded samples, subject to a restricted-access process to prevent misuse. Voice live and conversational features support building voice agents, and avatar capabilities create talking presenters from text. Container deployments allow running models on premises or at the edge, and the service integrates with Azure OpenAI and other Azure AI tools.

item.title: Google Cloud Text-to-Speech
item.description:
Google Cloud Text-to-Speech gives developers speech synthesis built on the technology behind Google’s assistants. A request with text returns audio in formats like MP3 or WAV, with a choice of voices and languages. The newer voice families, such as WaveNet and the Chirp generation, sound much more natural than traditional synthetic voices, and there are many accents and genders to choose from.

Developers can fine-tune delivery with SSML, adding pauses, emphasis, pronunciation, and speed. The service supports long audio synthesis for audiobooks and narration, and streaming for real-time applications such as voice assistants and interactive voice response systems. Customers can request a custom voice trained on their own recordings, with strict requirements, and the service integrates with other Google Cloud tools.

item.title: Milan Voice AI
item.description:
Milan Voice AI generates speech for creators and developers. Users type text and choose or create a voice, with options to clone a voice from a short sample or describe a new one. Multi-speaker mode takes a script with several characters and produces a dialogue, useful for podcasts, audiobooks, and videos.

Typical uses include narration, character voices, and prototypes of voice features. An API supports integration into apps. Voice cloning requires permission from the person whose voice is copied, and synthetic audio should be disclosed where appropriate.

item.title: Neets AI
item.description:
Neets AI offers speech synthesis through a simple API. Developers send text and choose a voice, and the service returns audio. It emphasizes variety of voices, speed, and low cost, which suits projects that generate large volumes of audio, such as reading articles aloud.

Typical users include app developers, content publishers, and teams building voice agents. Voice quality is good for many purposes, though the top-tier commercial providers may offer more emotion and control. Streaming support makes it usable for interactive applications.

item.title: Cartesia
item.description:
Cartesia focuses on speed in voice AI. Its Sonic models, built on state-space model architectures instead of only transformers, generate natural-sounding speech with very low latency, so a voice agent can start speaking almost as soon as a response is ready. That matters for phone calls and live assistants, where delays feel awkward. The company also offers voice cloning and control over emotion and speaking rate.

The platform has grown into a set of real-time voice building blocks. Sonic handles text-to-speech, Ink handles speech-to-text, and tools for managed voice agents help companies deploy agents that answer phone calls. Developers connect through APIs and SDKs, and Cartesia works with common voice agent frameworks and telephony providers. Multilingual support lets one system serve customers in different languages.

item.title: Hume AI
item.description: Hume AI started from research on human emotion. Its models analyze the way people speak and show emotion, including tone, pace, and inflection, and its Empathic Voice Interface (EVI) uses that understanding in a conversational voice assistant. EVI listens to the user’s voice, picks up on cues like frustration or excitement, and adjusts its responses and speaking style accordingly, so a voice agent can feel more natural than one that only transcribes words.

item.title: Lovo AI
item.description:
Lovo makes synthetic speech for creators and businesses. Users type or paste a script, choose a voice, and adjust tone, speed, and emphasis to generate narration. Genny, the editor, lets them place speech alongside video, images, and music in one timeline.

Voice cloning and a marketplace of voices expand the options, and the platform supports many languages. Typical uses are explainer videos, e-learning, ads, and audiobooks. An API provides access for developers.

item.title: WellSaid Labs
item.description:
WellSaid focuses on voiceovers for businesses. In its web studio, you type or paste a script, pick a voice, and generate narration with control over pacing, pronunciation, and emphasis. The voices are built from recordings by professional voice actors who agreed to the use, which gives companies a clear license position. Typical projects include training courses, explainer videos, product tours, corporate announcements, and audio for apps.

For larger teams, collaboration and control matter. Projects can be shared, commented on, and reviewed, and custom pronunciation settings keep brand names and technical terms consistent across a library of content. An API lets developers add speech to their own products, and integrations connect WellSaid to e-learning and creative tools. Enterprise plans emphasize security, privacy, and compliance, and custom voices can be created for a brand.

item.title: Fish Audio
item.description:
Fish Audio generates synthetic speech with an emphasis on voice variety. Users type text, choose a voice, and get audio. A cloning feature creates a voice from a short sample, and a public library offers voices shared by other users, including character and celebrity-style options.

Creators use it for narration, videos, games, and podcasts, and developers integrate it through an API for apps and agents. The company has released open models for speech synthesis, which has helped it build a community of users and researchers.

item.title: Amazon Polly
item.description:
Polly takes text and returns audio, which developers call from their apps to add speech. It offers dozens of voices across many languages and accents, built on several engines. The neural voices sound considerably more natural than the older standard ones, and newer generative voices push realism further. It is used for reading articles aloud, voicing phone systems and assistants, creating e-learning narration, and adding accessibility features to apps.

Control over how things are said is a strength. SSML tags let you adjust pauses, emphasis, pitch, speed, and the way numbers, dates, and abbreviations are spoken. Custom lexicons teach Polly the right pronunciation of brand names and jargon. It can also return speech marks that tell your app when each word is spoken, which is useful for highlighting text in sync with audio. Output can be streamed or saved as files in common formats.

item.title: Kokoro TTS
item.description:
Kokoro is notable for doing a lot with a little. The model is small enough to run on a laptop, a phone, or a modest server, yet produces speech that many listeners find clear and natural in several voices. That makes it practical for local and low-cost deployments.

Developers use it for narration, accessibility tools, voice agents, and offline applications, and community projects have packaged it for the browser and for popular frameworks. The license is permissive, which allows commercial use, and the weights are available on Hugging Face.

item.title: PlayHT
item.description: PlayHT offered realistic text-to-speech with a large catalog of voices across many languages, plus voice cloning from short audio samples. Creators used its web studio to narrate videos, podcasts, and audiobooks, and developers used its API to add speech to apps and phone systems. Its later conversational models were built to sound natural in dialogue, with emotion and pacing, and the company also developed voice agents under the PlayAI name.
